title: Empirical formulas
subtitle: Percentage composition, atom ratios and a molecular-formula extension
subject: Chemistry
syllabusDotPoints: explore the concept of the mole and relate this to Avogadro's constant to describe, calculate and manipulate numbers of particles, chemical amounts and masses
calculate percentage composition by mass of multi-element compounds
inquiryQuestion: How are measurements made in chemistry?
lessonIntent: Explain mass-to-mole ratio reasoning, derive an empirical formula and distinguish related molecular inference from substance identification.
examSkill: Convert element masses to moles, preserve ratios and interpret what composition data can establish.

scenes.heading: Same ratio, different substances
scenes.body: An empirical formula gives composition. It does not identify the substance.
scenes.callout: First find the ratio of atoms.
scenes.caption: Different substances can share an empirical formula.

voiceover.text: We already know how to turn grams into moles. Now we can use that idea to work backwards from a compound's composition. Glucose and formaldehyde are very different substances. Yet both have the same simplest ratio of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms: one to two to one. So a composition result can give us a useful clue without telling us exactly what the substance is. The first clue is an empirical formula. Let's see how a measurement of mass becomes a ratio of atoms.
Empirical formulas: from percentage composition to a ratio of atoms.

scenes.heading: Ratio versus actual count
scenes.body: Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio. Molecular formula: atoms in one molecule.
scenes.secondary: Counting model only. Blocks do not show bonds or separate glucose fragments.
scenes.caption: Empirical formulas preserve proportions; molecular formulas preserve actual counts.

voiceover.text: Glucose has six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens in each molecule. That six to twelve to six ratio reduces to one to two to one, written C H two O. Formaldehyde already has one carbon, two hydrogens and one oxygen. Its formula reduces to the same ratio. The empirical formula keeps the proportion. The molecular formula keeps the actual atom count in one molecule. These blocks are a counting model; they don't show how the atoms are bonded.

scenes.heading: Mass percentage
scenes.callout: Atom ratios and mass percentages describe different relationships.
scenes.caption: Mass percentage compares an element’s mass contribution with the total.

bullets.text: Mass percentage = element mass ÷ total mass × 100.

voiceover.text: Percentage composition measures a different relationship: how much of a compound's mass comes from each element. For C H two O, the carbon contributes twelve point zero one out of a total of thirty point zero two six grams per mole, using our supplied values. Divide the carbon contribution by the total, then multiply by one hundred. That's about forty percent carbon by mass. The hydrogen count is twice the carbon count, but hydrogen atoms are much lighter. Atom ratios and mass percentages won't generally be the same numbers.

scenes.heading: Mass to moles to ratio
scenes.body: A 100 g calculation basis turns each mass percentage into grams.

bullets.text: Choose a basis, or use the actual element masses supplied.
Convert each mass to moles using its own molar mass.

scenes.secondary: Schematic mass accounting. This is not physically separating a compound into elements.
scenes.callout: Moles put all elements on a common counting scale.
scenes.caption: A convenient basis changes sample size, not percentage composition.

voiceover.text: Suppose an analysis gives forty point zero zero percent carbon, six point seven one percent hydrogen and fifty-three point two nine percent oxygen. A hundred-gram calculation basis makes those percentages easy to use: forty grams, six point seven one grams and fifty-three point two nine grams. We haven't changed the composition, just chosen a convenient sample size. If actual element masses are already given, use them directly. Next, dividing each mass by its own molar mass puts all three elements onto a common counting scale: moles.

scenes.heading: Find the empirical formula
scenes.question: Composition: 40.00% C, 6.71% H, 53.29% O. Find the empirical formula. Use C 12.01, H 1.008, O 16.00 g mol⁻¹.
scenes.coachNote: Use a 100 g basis and retain guard digits.
steps: Convert the elemental masses to moles
Divide by the smallest unrounded amount
scenes.caption: Masses must become mole amounts before comparing atom ratios.

voiceover.text: The board shows those three conversions. Carbon gives about three point three three moles, hydrogen about six point six six, and oxygen about three point three three. Hydrogen's smaller mass contains nearly twice as many atoms. Dividing every amount by the smallest keeps their proportions but makes them easier to recognise. With the extra digits retained, the ratio is very close to one, two, one. So the empirical formula is C H two O.

calculationPresentation.note: Choose a 100 g calculation basis. Retain unrounded amounts for the ratios.

Recognise the simplest whole-number ratio
stages.summary: One carbon, two hydrogens, one oxygen

scenes.heading: Extension: molecular formula
scenes.question: For a single molecular substance with empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 180.16 g mol⁻¹, find its molecular formula.
scenes.coachNote: Molar mass supplies the scale. A formula does not uniquely identify a substance.
steps: Result is consistent with glucose, but does not identify it.
scenes.caption: Molecular-formula inference is a related extension to the empirical-formula core.

voiceover.text: If the question also supplies a molecular molar mass, we can go one step further. Here it is one hundred and eighty point one six grams per mole. The empirical-formula molar mass is thirty point zero two six grams per mole. The supplied molar mass is about six times that value, so every subscript is multiplied by six. We get C six H twelve O six. Glucose has that molecular formula, but the formula alone doesn't prove the substance is glucose. How those atoms are arranged still matters.

Find the whole-number multiplier
stages.summary: Molecular formula is 6 times the empirical ratio

Keep the identification claim limited
lines: The formula alone does not identify a substance.
stages.summary: Formula is composition, not a unique identity

phases.label: Formula alone does not identify the substance
Atom arrangement matters
lines: Same formula can describe different substances.

scenes.heading: Keep the proportion
scenes.body: Wrong: round 1:1.5 to 1:2. That changes the ratio.
scenes.secondary: Correct: multiply both terms by 2 to get 2:3. The ratio stays the same.
scenes.callout: Preserve every term together. Check unexpected ratios.
scenes.caption: Multiplying all ratio terms preserves their proportions.

voiceover.text: A ratio of one to one point five can look awkward, but rounding it to one to two changes the proportion. Multiplying both values by two gives two to three and preserves it. The same idea helps with thirds and quarters. Keep the calculation digits until you can judge the pattern. Small departures from whole numbers can come from rounded measurements; an unexpected result is a reason to check the data, not force an answer.

scenes.heading: A new pair of elements
scenes.question: Approximately 30.45% N and 69.55% O by mass. Find the empirical formula. Use N 14.01 and O 16.00 g mol⁻¹.
answerSteps: Divide both mole amounts by the smaller
scenes.caption: Find the simplest whole-number ratio from these mass percentages.

voiceover.text: Try a new pair of elements. A compound contains approximately thirty point four five percent nitrogen and sixty-nine point five five percent oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula, using the supplied molar masses. Pause here if you'd like time to calculate it. On a hundred-gram basis, the nitrogen gives about two point one seven moles and the oxygen about four point three five. Dividing by the nitrogen amount gives approximately one to two. The empirical formula is N O two. If you compared the two masses directly, oxygen would look like just over twice the nitrogen. Converting to moles is what makes that comparison about atoms.

scenes.heading: From mass to atom ratio
points: Choose a basis, or use the supplied element masses.
Compare mole amounts to infer the simplest whole-number ratio.
Molecular molar mass supplies scale, but not unique identity.
scenes.finalPrompt: Preserve the ratio. Check what the data actually establish.
scenes.caption: An empirical formula describes a ratio, not a complete substance identification.

voiceover.text: Composition questions connect mass to atom ratios. Choose a convenient basis, convert each element to moles, then find the simplest whole-number ratio without rounding the proportion away. A molecular molar mass can supply the scale for a molecular formula. And remember our starting puzzle: a ratio is a clue to composition, not a complete identification of the substance. Next, a balanced equation lets us compare amounts of different substances in a reaction. That is a different ratio, and it is where stoichiometry begins.
